blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: On-policy distillation consolidates specialist models into one student at the price of rollouts, teacher passes and gradient steps for every teacher. We show that the consolidation does not need training: with forward passes only, the capabilities of separately tuned specialists can be aggregated into one model that is, on average, more accurate than either specialist alone. When specialists share a base model, distillation has an exact layer-wise solution: each linear layer of the fused model must reproduce every specialist's output on the inputs that specialist receives while reading its own answers, a least-squares problem whose solution needs only the second moments of those inputs. One forward pass over a few hundred rollouts provides them. We call this training-free on-policy distillation (\method). What the rollouts contain matters more than the solver: answers truncated in repetition loops are few among a mathematics specialist's rollouts but carry a large share of their tokens, and removing them lifts the fused model on AIME25 from task arithmetic's level to the specialist's at matched precision. On Olmo~3 7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist yield a generalist that keeps most of each specialist's gain on each of seven mathematics and code benchmarks.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards has become the standard way to
turn a base language model into a strong reasoner in one domain [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] .
Because the reward is domain-specific, the result is a family of specialists
that share an initialization: from one base checkpoint, one model is trained
on competition mathematics, another on programming, a third on instruction
following [ 6 ] . Each is far ahead on its own domain and far
behind on the others, so a user who wants mathematics and programming in the
same model has to build that model from the specialists.

blocks.en:
We connect the two lines. For a single linear layer, asking the fused weight
to reproduce each teacher’s output on that teacher’s inputs is the
distillation objective restricted to the layer, and it is the least-squares
problem that RegMean solves: once the second moments of the inputs are known,
no optimization is left to run. TF-OPD gathers those moments where on-policy
distillation gathers its data, on rollouts. Each specialist answers a few
hundred training problems from its domain, the answers are filtered, the
specialist reads its kept answers once with teacher forcing while forward
hooks accumulate a Gram matrix per layer, and each layer is then solved
exactly. Nothing is back-propagated.

On Olmo 3 7B this yields a generalist without a single gradient step: one
model that keeps most of what each specialist gained on five mathematics and
two code benchmarks and that is, on average, more accurate than either
specialist alone (Figure 1 ).
Three findings explain when it
works. First, the filter carries the result. A minority of the mathematics
specialist’s rollouts run to the length limit in a repetition loop: few among
the answers, several times more among the tokens. With them the closed form is
no better than task arithmetic on AIME25, and removing them alone closes the
gap to the specialist scored in the same format. Second, the token-level fit is
not what fails: the unfiltered model already follows the specialist almost
token for token, so hard problems are decided by which inputs the statistics
weigh. Third, rollouts written by the student, the on-policy data of trained
distillation, do not improve the closed form. Reinforcement learning also
moves weights so little that the 16-bit release format distorts a fused
update, which makes the formats of storage and evaluation part of the method.

blocks.en:
• We show that the capabilities of separately tuned specialists can be
aggregated without training. On Olmo 3 7B, a closed-form fusion of a
mathematics and a coding specialist keeps most of each specialist’s gain on
seven benchmarks and is, on average, more accurate than either specialist
alone, after a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist. • The method, TF-OPD, reads layer-wise distillation from several
teachers as the closed-form problem of RegMean and feeds it statistics from
the specialists’ own rollouts, using forward passes only. • We show that the composition of those rollouts decides the outcome on
hard problems. Truncated answers ending in repetition loops are a small share
of answers and a large share of tokens, and removing them separates a fused
model that falls short of its mathematics specialist from one that matches it
in the same evaluation format. • We analyze what matters and what does not: a close token-level fit does
not protect hard problems; student rollouts, domain reweighting and mined
hard problems do not improve on selection; numerical precision does.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Classical distillation fits a student to a
teacher’s output distribution on a fixed corpus [ 15 ] or to sequences the teacher generates [ 16 ] . On-policy
formulations supervise text generated by the model being trained, following
the imitation-learning argument for learning on the learner’s own state
distribution [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] ; the idea has
been applied to reasoning models, including with a model as its own teacher [ 17 ] , and knowledge fusion extends distillation to several
source models [ 18 ] . Recent work asks which rollouts
on-policy distillation should use, selecting a few hard problems [ 19 ] , weighting problems by the student’s pass rate [ 20 ] , or balancing student-generated states across teachers [ 12 ] . All of these are optimization procedures. TF-OPD keeps
two of their ingredients, a match-the-teacher objective and statistics
gathered on model-generated text, and removes the optimization by solving the
objective layer by layer. Our finding that the composition of the rollouts
decides the outcome is a closed-form counterpart of theirs.

blocks.en:
Weight averaging across fine-tuning runs improves
accuracy at no inference cost [ 21 ] ; task arithmetic
composes updates relative to a common initialization [ 13 ] ,
and TIES-Merging and DARE reduce interference among summed updates [ 22 , 23 ] . Spectral methods exploit the matrix structure
of updates [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] . These
methods read weights only. Weight-space edits also target reasoning models,
to amplify one reinforcement-learning run [ 27 ] or to make a model more
efficient [ 28 ] ; we combine runs on different
domains. Fisher merging and RegMean bring in data through parameter
importance and through input second moments respectively [ 29 , 14 ] . TF-OPD uses RegMean’s closed form;
what differs is what it is fed and what it is used for. RegMean was introduced
for models fine-tuned on supervised tasks, with statistics computed on each
task’s training inputs. The specialists here are reinforcement-learned
reasoners whose inputs are overwhelmingly their own long generations, so the
statistics have to come from rollouts, and we show that on AIME25 unfiltered
rollouts gain nothing over task arithmetic, whereas filtered ones recover the
specialist.

blocks.en:
Every token of every kept answer contributes one outer product to G d G_{d} , so

picture is distorted by a failure mode of long-form generation. Some answers

and the layer inputs inside a loop are nearly periodic, so their contribution
to the Gram matrix is large and concentrated on a few directions. The
least-squares solution then spends its capacity reproducing the teacher on
degenerate input.

blocks.en:
Released checkpoints are stored in bfloat16, which keeps eight significant
bits. Reinforcement learning with small learning rates barely moves weights at
that resolution, by about one representable step
(Section 4.5 ). A fused update is no larger, and unlike a
specialist’s it is not made of whole steps. We therefore store fused models
in 32-bit floats, since rounding the fused update to bfloat16 measurably
distorts it. A fused model is evaluated in float16, which keeps three more
significant bits than bfloat16 and fits the memory of a single GPU where
float32 does not. A format change by itself shifts measured accuracy, so we
state the format behind every score.

specialists that share a base model, the closed form reaches a consolidated
model at roughly the cost of collecting such data once. Its advantage over
weight arithmetic is on hard problems: task arithmetic costs even less, but
falls short on AIME25, where the closed form with clean rollouts matches the
specialist in the same format (Section 4.5 ).

blocks.en: 4.6 Discussion
blocks.zh: 4.6 讨论情况

blocks.en:
On-policy distillation is run after reinforcement learning to put several
specialists into one model. For specialists that share a base model, our
results suggest that the training in that step may not be needed. What the
trained student is asked to do, match each teacher on the text the models
generate, has an exact layer-wise solution, and that solution already gives a
model close to each teacher and more accurate on average than either. Adding
a specialist then costs its rollouts and one more term in each layer’s sums;
nothing is retrained. Training remains the tool when the teachers differ in
architecture or size from the student.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
Aggregating the capabilities of separately tuned specialists does not require
training-based on-policy distillation when they share a base model, and the
aggregate can be more accurate on average than any of its sources.
For a linear layer the distillation objective is least squares, its solution is
exact given the second moments of each teacher’s inputs, and those are
obtained by letting the teachers read a few hundred of their own answers, at
the cost of forward passes. What those answers contain decides the hard
problems: removing a few looping answers, which carry a large share of the
tokens, lets the fused model match its mathematics specialist in the same
format.
